title: Fw 190 D-9 Dora (DCS)

sources.title: DCS Fw 190 D-9 Flight Manual (EN)
sources.file: Mods/aircraft/FW-190D9/Doc/DCS Fw 190 D-9 Flight Manual EN.pdf

intro: The Fw 190 D-9 is a German single-seat fighter of World War II with a long nose and a liquid-cooled engine. The cockpit is built so that the pilot reaches the important things by hand: engine, radio, flaps and landing gear on the left, the circuit breakers on the right and the instruments in front. A mechanical engine computer sets most engine details, so the pilot mainly moves the throttle.

areas.name: Gunsight and weapons
areas.text: Straight in front of the pilot's eyes sits the EZ 42 gunsight, with the SZKK 4 ammunition counters below it. The weapon console with the bomb and rocket switches is on the lower front panel.

panels.name: EZ 42 gunsight (Einheitszielvorrichtung)
panels.text: The EZ 42 is the sight the pilot looks through to aim the guns. A glass plate shows a ring and a dot in the pilot's view. The sight works out by itself where the bullets must go to hit a moving target.
panels.context: An analog computer with a gyroscope (a spinning wheel that senses turning) measures how the plane turns. The pilot sets the target's size and the range, and the sight then moves the aiming mark to the right lead point.

controls.name: Gunsight reticle (floating aiming ring)
controls.text: This is the aiming mark on the glass: a ring with a dot in the middle. The mark floats and moves by itself to show where the shots will go. The pilot lays the ring around the enemy plane.
controls.context: The ring's size is matched to the enemy's wingspan and range. When the enemy just fills the ring, the sight has the distance it needs for the lead calculation.

controls.name: Night filter lever

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The filter is out of the way.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The filter is in front of the sight glass.

controls.text: This lever swings a filter in front of the sight glass. The game calls it 'Night Lens Filter' and gives it an ON and an OFF command.
controls.context: It is meant for flying in the dark. The manual only lists the part by name.

controls.name: Brightness lever
controls.text: This control sets how bright the aiming mark on the glass is. The game names it 'EZ42 Gunsight Brightness Control'.
controls.context: A brighter mark helps in bright daylight, a dimmer one is easier on the eyes in the dark.

controls.name: Target wingspan knob
controls.text: With this knob the pilot tells the sight how wide the enemy plane is. The scale runs from 10 to 40 metres. Three marks show typical wingspans: 11.5 m for a single-engine fighter, 16.5 m for a twin-engine plane and 31.8 m for a four-engine bomber.
controls.context: The pilot sets it at the first sight of an enemy, as exactly as possible. Then he turns the range twist grip on the throttle until the target fills the ring.

controls.name: Gunsight gyro power switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The gyroscope is off and the sight cannot compute the lead.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The gyroscope runs up and feeds the sight.

controls.text: This switch turns on the electric gyroscope inside the sight. Without a running gyro the sight cannot work out the lead.
controls.context: The manual says the gyro needs about 1.5 minutes to run up. The pilot switches it on early, together with the guns master arm switch, before an attack.

controls.name: Range scale indicator
controls.text: This pointer on the right of the sight shows the range that the pilot has set, from 0 to 1000 metres. It moves when the range twist grip on the throttle is turned.
controls.context: A cable joins the twist grip and the sight. The set range is one of the inputs the sight uses to compute the lead.

controls.name: Backup iron sight (Kimme and Korn)
controls.text: These are two simple metal sights for aiming without electricity. The rear sight, the Kimme, is a Y-shaped pin at the front left of the sight. The front sight, the Korn, is the arrow-shaped end of the glass holder.
controls.context: The pilot lines up the tip of the arrow with the tips of the Y to point the guns at the target if the sight does not work.

panels.name: SZKK 4 ammunition counter and gun controls
panels.text: This box shows how much ammunition is left for each of the four guns and whether the guns are working. A master arm switch arms the guns.
panels.context: German pilots could see their ammunition in the cockpit. The counters are not linked to the real ammunition. They are set to full on the ground and drop one notch with every shot.

controls.name: SZKK 4 ammunition counters
controls.text: Four vertical bars show the ammunition of the four guns, from left to right: left MG 151, left MG 131, right MG 131 and right MG 151. The white part of a bar is ammunition left, the black part is used up.
controls.context: The outer bars belong to the wing guns, the inner two to the guns above the engine.

controls.name: Gun 1-4 ammunition count knobs
controls.text: These four knobs set the ammunition counter of one gun each. The game names them 'Set Gun 1 to 4 Ammunition Count'.
controls.context: The manual says the counters are set to full when the guns are loaded on the ground. It does not describe these knobs in detail.

controls.name: Left MG 151 lock control indicator
controls.text: This mechanical flag on top of the left MG 151 counter shows the state of that cannon's breechblock (the part that closes the gun). Black means closed, light means open.
controls.context: It flickers while the gun fires. If it stays black or light after the trigger is pressed, the gun has a fault.

controls.name: Lock control lamp panel (Rumpf / Flügel)
controls.text: These red lamps show the state of the other guns' breechblocks. The lamp marked Rumpf (fuselage) is for the two MG 131 guns. The lamp marked Flügel (wing) is for the right MG 151.
controls.context: A lamp flickers while its guns fire. A lamp that stays on or off when the trigger is pressed points to a gun fault.

controls.name: Guns master arm switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The guns are safe.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: The guns are armed and the trigger fires them.

controls.text: This switch arms the guns. Until it is on, the trigger on the stick does not fire.
controls.context: It is the first step of the gun procedure in the manual, followed by the gyro power switch of the gunsight.

panels.name: Weapons console (rockets and bombs)
panels.text: This small console on the lower front panel has the rocket switches, four load lamps and the bomb fusing dial. It is used for bombs and rockets, not for the guns.
panels.context: The pilot sets the bomb dial before a bombing run. Bombs and rockets are fired later with the B2 button on the stick.

controls.name: 21-cm rocket control unit
controls.text: This is the upper part of the weapons console. It holds two switches for the 21-cm rockets under the wings: a main switch and an emergency release switch.
controls.context: The two switches are explained one by one below.

controls.name: Main rocket switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Aus: the rockets are safe.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Ein: the rockets are armed.

controls.text: This switch arms or disarms the underwing rockets. With the switch at Aus, pressing the B2 button on the stick launches nothing.
controls.context: The pilot turns it on only when about to fire rockets. The rockets are then launched with the B2 button.

controls.name: Rocket emergency release switch

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Aus: safe, nothing is jettisoned.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Ein: the explosive bolts detach the rocket launchers from the wings.

controls.text: This switch blasts the rocket launchers off the wings so that the plane flies clean again. A safety plate that must be bent aside first protects it.
controls.context: It is an emergency measure, for example if the rockets get in the way. At Aus the switch is safe.

controls.name: Disposable load indicator lights
controls.text: Four lamps under the rocket switches show which loads the plane still carries. The manual does not say more about them.
controls.context: They are part of the weapons console.

controls.name: Bomb fusing selector (ZSK 244)

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Aus: the bomb release is disarmed.

positions.name: Sturz MV
positions.text: Dive bombing, with delay: the bomb explodes a short moment after impact.

positions.name: Sturz OV
positions.text: Dive bombing, without delay: the bomb explodes on impact.

positions.name: Wagerecht MV
positions.text: Level bombing, with delay: the bomb explodes a short moment after impact.

positions.name: Wagerecht OV
positions.text: Level bombing, without delay: the bomb explodes on impact.

controls.text: This dial decides how a bomb's fuse is armed and when it goes off. At Aus (off) the bomb release is disarmed. Sturz is for dive bombing, Wagerecht for level bombing. OV means the bomb goes off at once on impact, MV after a short delay.
controls.context: The pilot sets it before the bombing run, because it must match the attack. The bombs are dropped later with the B2 button on the stick.

areas.name: Main instrument panel (front dash)
areas.text: Flight instruments are in the middle and engine gauges below and to the right. The lower part holds the fuel, radiator and emergency handles.

panels.name: Flight instruments
panels.text: These dials tell the pilot how fast the plane flies, how high, whether it climbs or sinks and which way it points.
panels.context: The pilot scans them all the time in flight. In bad weather they are the only way to know the plane's position in the air.

controls.name: Airspeed indicator (km/h)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the plane moves through the air, in kilometres per hour. A needle points to the number. The numbers overlap at the bottom of the dial, so the pilot uses common sense to tell a slow speed from a very fast one.
controls.context: The pilot watches it all the time: for take-off, for landing and to keep out of speeds that could damage the plane.

controls.name: Vertical speed indicator (variometer)
controls.text: This dial shows whether the plane is climbing or sinking and how quickly, in metres per second. The needle points up for climbing and down for sinking.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to hold the height steadily in a turn or to climb or descend at a calm, steady rate.

panels.name: Altitude indicator (altimeter)
panels.text: This dial shows the height of the plane above the ground level that the pilot set. A needle shows hundreds of metres. A small window shows whole kilometres.
panels.context: The pilot adds the kilometre disk and the needle: disk 3 and needle at 0.4 means 3400 metres.

controls.name: Altimeter needle, kilometre disk and pressure window
controls.text: The long needle shows the height in tens of metres within one kilometre. The lower window shows the whole kilometres, the upper window the air pressure in millibar that the gauge is set to.
controls.context: It measures air pressure, so it needs the sea level knob to read the right height.

controls.name: Altimeter pressure setting knob
controls.text: This knob sets the air pressure that the height gauge uses as its starting point. Turning it moves the pressure number in the small window. The game names it 'Altimeter Pressure Set'.
controls.context: Before take-off the pilot sets it so that the gauge reads the right height for the airfield.

panels.name: Artificial horizon / turn and bank indicator
panels.text: This one instrument holds a horizon, a turn needle and a slip ball. It shows the pilot the plane's tilt when the real horizon cannot be seen.
panels.context: The pilot uses it for flying by instruments. The outer ring locks and frees the gyroscope inside.

controls.name: Artificial horizon / turn and bank indicator
controls.text: This instrument shows the pilot how the plane sits in the air when clouds or darkness hide the real horizon. A bar shows nose-up or nose-down and the tilt of the wings. A needle shows how fast the plane turns, and a ball in a curved tube shows whether the turn is clean.
controls.context: The pilot uses it for flying by instruments. The manual notes that its horizon bar is locked during aerobatics.

controls.name: Horizon cage ring (Fest / Los)
controls.text: This ring on the artificial horizon locks or frees its inner gyroscope (a spinning wheel that keeps the horizon steady). The word Fest on the dial means locked (caged). The word Los means free (uncaged).
controls.context: The pilot sets it to Los (free) for normal flying so that the horizon works.

panels.name: Repeater compass
panels.text: This dial shows the plane's heading, the direction it flies. The compass rose can be turned to mark the wanted heading.
panels.context: The pilot flies a planned route by holding the pointer on the wanted heading.

controls.name: Repeater compass
controls.text: This compass shows the direction the plane is heading. A small plane symbol with a pointer turns as the plane changes direction. A marked stripe on the dial can be set to the heading the pilot wants to fly.
controls.context: The pilot keeps the pointer on the wanted heading to fly a planned route.

controls.name: Compass bezel (desired heading)
controls.text: This turnable ring around the compass moves the compass rose. The pilot turns it until the reference stripe sits on the heading he wants to fly. The game names this control 'Course Set'.
controls.context: After setting the stripe, the pilot only has to keep the pointer on it to hold the course.

panels.name: AFN-2 homing indicator
panels.text: This small dial points the pilot to a radio beacon on the ground and shows how far it is.
panels.context: It belongs to the FuG 16ZY radio. Its frequency can be set in the mission editor, by default 38 MHz.

controls.name: AFN-2 homing indicator
controls.text: This small dial points the way to a radio beacon on the ground. A vertical bar shows whether the beacon lies left or right of the nose. A horizontal bar shows how far away it is. A lamp in the middle lights when the plane flies over the beacon's marker.
controls.context: It is part of the FuG 16ZY radio set. The pilot follows it to find an airfield when the ground is hidden.

controls.name: AFN-2 marker lamp, distance bar and direction bar
controls.text: The vertical bar shows whether the beacon is to the left or right of the nose. The horizontal bar shows the distance. The lamp in the middle lights when the plane flies over the near or far marker beacon of an airfield.
controls.context: Strong vibration can disturb this sensitive instrument.

panels.name: FuG 25a IFF control unit
panels.text: IFF stands for identification friend or foe. The unit answers a ground radar so that the radar knows the plane is friendly.
panels.context: In the D-9 the manual lists this unit as not implemented. The game still has two clickable parts.

controls.name: FuG 25a IFF control unit (not implemented)
controls.text: This is the control box of the FuG 25a identification system. The D-9 manual marks it as not implemented.
controls.context: In real life it answered the radar stations Freya and Würzburg with a coded signal.

controls.name: IFF channel selector
controls.text: The game names this switch 'IFF Channel Selector'. The manual does not describe it, and says the unit is not implemented.
controls.context: Do not expect a function from this control in the D-9.

controls.name: IFF check button
controls.text: The game names this button 'IFF Check'. The manual does not describe it, and says the unit is not implemented.
controls.context: Do not expect a function from this control in the D-9.

panels.name: Engine gauges
panels.text: These dials show how the engine is doing: how hard the supercharger pushes, how fast the engine turns and the pressures and temperatures of fuel, oil, coolant and the MW-50 liquid.
panels.context: The pilot checks them after the engine start and in flight. A needle outside its marked strip means trouble.

controls.name: Supercharger pressure gauge (ATA)
controls.text: This gauge shows how hard the supercharger (a pump that pushes extra air into the engine) is pressing. The unit is ATA, an old measure of air pressure. The more pressure, the more power the engine gives.
controls.context: In this plane the throttle lever is moved until this gauge shows the wanted pressure. It is one of the most important engine gauges.

controls.name: Tachometer (RPM x 100)
controls.text: This dial shows how fast the engine turns, in hundreds of revolutions per minute (RPM). A reading of 24 means 2400 turns every minute.
controls.context: The engine control unit sets the engine speed by itself from the throttle position, so the pilot mostly watches this dial to check that everything runs as it should.

controls.name: Fuel and oil pressure gauge
controls.text: This double gauge shows two things. The left needle shows the pressure of the fuel, the right needle the pressure of the engine oil. Marked strips show the normal range.
controls.context: The pilot checks it after the engine starts and from time to time in flight. A needle outside its strip points to engine trouble.

controls.name: Coolant temperature gauge
controls.text: This dial shows how hot the engine's cooling liquid is, in degrees Celsius. The normal range is marked on the dial.
controls.context: The D-9 has a liquid-cooled engine, so this is a key gauge. The manual says to watch it at all times to avoid overheating.

controls.name: Oil temperature gauge
controls.text: This dial shows how hot the engine oil is, in degrees Celsius. Marked strips show the normal range.
controls.context: The pilot lets the oil warm up before demanding full power and watches that it does not get too hot.

controls.name: Water/methanol pressure gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows the pressure of the MW-50 liquid, a mix of water and methanol that is sprayed into the engine for extra power.
controls.context: The MW-50 switch has no light, so the pilot can see that the system runs by watching this gauge, the supercharger gauge and the engine sound.

panels.name: Fuel contents gauge and warning lights
panels.text: These parts show how much fuel is in the two main tanks and warn when a tank is nearly empty.
panels.context: There is one gauge for two tanks. A switch chooses which tank the gauge reports.

controls.name: Fuel contents gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows how much fuel is in one of the two main tanks. The selector switch next to it chooses the tank. The upper scale is for the rear tank, the lower scale for the front tank.
controls.context: The gauge does not show a drop tank or an extra fuselage tank. While those are feeding the rear tank, the rear tank reads full.

controls.name: Fuel gauge selector switch

positions.name: Vorn
positions.text: The fuel contents gauge shows the front tank.

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: The game offers this third position; the manual does not describe it.

positions.name: Hinten
positions.text: The fuel contents gauge shows the rear tank.

controls.text: This switch chooses which fuel tank the fuel contents gauge reports: the front tank (Vorn) or the rear tank (Hinten). In the game it also has an OFF position.
controls.context: The pilot checks both tanks before starting. With a drop tank fitted, the manual says to set it to Hinten.

controls.name: Fuel warning lights (vorn / hinten)
controls.text: Two lamps warn of low fuel. The red lamp marked vorn lights when the front tank is down to 80 litres. The white lamp marked hinten lights when the rear tank is down to 10 litres.
controls.context: The white lamp means it is time to switch over from the rear tank. The pilot then keeps an eye on the fuel left.

panels.name: Lower front dash: radiator, fuel and emergency handles
panels.text: Below the instruments are the handles for the radiator flaps, the fuel tank lever and the emergency pull handles.
panels.context: Most are used on the ground or only in an emergency.

controls.name: Radiator flap control (Zu / Auf)
controls.text: This hand wheel opens or closes the radiator flaps, the doors that let cooling air flow through the engine's radiator. Turned clockwise toward Auf (open) the flaps open. Turned counter-clockwise toward Zu (closed) they close. It is hidden behind the dashboard.
controls.context: The manual says to taxi and take off with the flaps fully open. There is no indicator in the cockpit that shows their position.

controls.name: Fuel tank selector lever

positions.name: Auf
positions.text: Both lines are open. The engine can take fuel from the front and the rear tank.

positions.name: Vorderer Behälter zu
positions.text: The front tank line is closed. The engine takes fuel from the rear tank only.

positions.name: Hinterer Behälter zu
positions.text: The rear tank line is closed. The engine takes fuel from the front tank only.

positions.name: Zu
positions.text: Both lines are closed. No fuel reaches the engine.

controls.text: This lever opens or closes the fuel lines from the two main tanks to the engine. Up (Auf) lets the engine drink from both. The other settings close the front line, the rear line, or both.
controls.context: The lever normally stays on Auf. The plane then empties its tanks in a sensible order by itself, so the pilot does not juggle tanks.

controls.name: Landing gear manual release handle
controls.text: Pulling this handle unlocks the landing gear by hand so that the wheels drop down under their own weight. The game has a command for pulling it and one for pushing it back.
controls.context: It is the back-up when the normal gear buttons fail. The plane should fly wings level so the wheels can fall into place.

controls.name: MBG emergency mode handle (Notzug)
controls.text: This handle is joined by a cable to the engine control unit (the MBG, Motorbediengerät). Pushed in, the control unit runs by itself. Pulled out, it allows the engine to run at higher boost than normal.
controls.context: It is for emergencies. The manual warns to watch engine speed and boost closely in this mode. If possible the handle should be pulled with the throttle at idle.

controls.name: Emergency fuselage load release handle
controls.text: Pulling this handle drops the load that hangs under the fuselage, such as a bomb or the drop tank (extra fuel tank). The word on the plate is Rumpflast or Bomben. The game names it 'Jettison Fuselage Stores'.
controls.context: It is an emergency tool, for example to get rid of bombs or the drop tank quickly.

controls.name: Emergency wing load release handle (Flügellast)
controls.text: Pulling this handle drops the loads hanging under the wings. The word on the plate is Flügellast. The game has no clickable part for it.
controls.context: It is an emergency tool next to the fuselage load release.

controls.name: Cold start and window rinsing (not implemented)
controls.text: The game names this control 'Cold Start/Wind Screen Washer'. The manual says it is not implemented, so it does nothing in DCS.
controls.context: In the real plane it helped starting a cold engine and cleaned the windscreen.

panels.name: Oxygen controls
panels.text: The oxygen system gives the pilot air to breathe high up. It has a valve, a flow indicator and a pressure gauge on the right of the front panel.
panels.context: The valve is turned on early in the cockpit routine. A separate emergency knob is explained in the rear area.

controls.name: Oxygen flow valve
controls.text: This knob opens the oxygen for the pilot's mask. Turned on, the oxygen runs to a regulator that mixes it with the outside air. Turned off, no oxygen flows.
controls.context: Oxygen is needed high up where the air is thin. The manual lists turning this valve on among the first things to do in the cockpit.

controls.name: Oxygen flow indicator
controls.text: This small window shows that oxygen is flowing. When the pilot breathes in, the flaps (blinkers) inside open. When the pilot breathes out, they close.
controls.context: If the blinkers stay still while the valve is open, the pilot knows something is wrong with the oxygen supply.

controls.name: Oxygen pressure gauge
controls.text: This gauge shows how much oxygen is left in the bottles, as a pressure. A full system reads about 150 kg per square centimetre.
controls.context: A fast drop while flying level or descending is not normal and can mean a leak. The reading also changes a little with the cold of high altitude.

areas.name: Left console
areas.text: The left side holds the engine and radio controls: ignition, MW-50, primer, radio panel and the electric kill-switch. The throttle, the flap and gear buttons and the trim switch are in the Stick and throttle section.

panels.name: Engine and system controls (left side)
panels.text: These controls on the left side start, power and protect the engine and the electrics.
panels.context: The ignition switch and primer are used during start-up. The MW-50 switch is used for emergency power.

controls.name: Ignition (magneto) selector switch

positions.text: Both magnetos are off. No sparks, the engine cannot run.

positions.name: M1
positions.text: Only the right magneto is used.

positions.name: M2
positions.text: Only the left magneto is used.

positions.name: M1+2
positions.text: Both magnetos are used. This is the normal setting.

controls.text: This switch chooses which magnetos (small generators that make the sparks for the engine) are in use. There are two for safety. The normal setting is both.
controls.context: The pilot sets it to M1+2 for the engine start and back to 0 to stop the engine.

controls.name: Primer pump handle
controls.text: This handle is a small hand pump. Each stroke squirts a little fuel into the engine to help it start.
controls.context: The pilot uses it while starting the engine. The manual's D-9 start-up list does not mention it.

controls.name: MW-B4 tank contents selector
controls.text: This selector tells the plane what is in the extra MW-50 tank: the water-methanol mix or normal aviation fuel (B4). The game labels it 'Not Functional'.
controls.context: The manual warns that a wrong setting could have catastrophic results, because it could feed water-methanol into the fuel lines or fuel into the supercharger.

controls.name: MW-50 power switch (Aus / Ein)

positions.name: OFF
positions.text: Aus: MW-50 injection is disabled.

positions.name: ON
positions.text: Ein: the system is enabled. The engine control unit adds MW-50 when the conditions are right and stops it when it is no longer needed.

controls.text: This switch enables the MW-50 system. MW-50 is a mix of water and methanol sprayed into the supercharger. It cools the air and allows much more boost, so the engine makes a lot more power.
controls.context: The tank pump must first be switched on with the E96 circuit breaker. There is no on-off lamp, so the pilot watches the gauges and listens to the engine.

controls.name: Instrument lighting control
controls.text: This knob makes the lighting of the instrument panel brighter or dimmer. The game offers an increase and a decrease command for it.
controls.context: It is used in the dark, so the dials can be read without glare.

controls.name: Electric kill-switch
controls.text: This switch shuts down the plane's whole electrical system in an emergency. In the game the command is called 'Electric Emergency Disconnect'.
controls.context: It is for emergencies only. After it is used the electric devices no longer get power.

controls.name: Equipment destruction button
controls.text: The game names this button 'Emergency Equipment Destruction'. The manual does not describe it. It lists only a radio self-destruction button that is not implemented.
controls.context: Do not expect a function from this control.

controls.name: Radio self-destruction button (not implemented)
controls.text: The manual lists this button as not implemented, so it does nothing in DCS.
controls.context: It is a spot in the cockpit that the real plane had.

controls.name: Heated suit connector (not implemented)
controls.text: This plug was for the electric heating of the pilot's flight suit. The manual lists it as not implemented, so it does nothing in DCS.
controls.context: It is only a part of the left wall.

controls.name: Throttle friction knob
controls.text: This knob sits under the throttle lever near the cockpit floor. Turning it makes the lever stiffer so it stays where the pilot put it.
controls.context: The pilot tightens it once the wanted engine setting is found, so the lever does not creep.

controls.name: Throttle lock
controls.text: The game names this control 'Throttle Lock'. The manual does not describe it.
controls.context: It sits in the group called Engine System in the game.

panels.name: FuG 16ZY radio controls
panels.text: The FuG 16ZY is the plane's radio. These four controls tune it, set the volume and switch between talking and homing.
panels.context: The microphone push-to-talk button is on the throttle. The AFN-2 dial on the front panel belongs to the same radio.

controls.name: FuG 16ZY frequency selector

positions.name: I
positions.text: Flight (management) frequency. The manual says it is not used in this simulation.

positions.name: II
positions.text: Group order frequency, for talking between several flights in a raid.

positions.name: III
positions.text: Airfield (air traffic control) frequency, for talking to the tower.

positions.name: IV
positions.text: Reich fighter defence frequency, for coordinating the national air defence.

controls.text: This switch picks one of four stored radio frequencies, like the station buttons of a car radio. The four frequencies are fixed before the flight in the mission editor. The pilot cannot type in new ones.
controls.context: Position I is for the pilot's own flight and is not used in this simulation. The next positions are for the group, the airfield tower and the national air defence.

controls.name: FuG 16ZY fine tuning knob
controls.text: This knob changes the radio's frequency in small steps around the chosen preset. The game calls it 'Radio Tuning (+/-30 kHz)'. The frequency is the 'station number' the radio talks on.
controls.context: It is a fine adjustment inside the frequency preset that the selector has picked.

controls.name: Headphone volume control
controls.text: This knob sets how loud the radio sounds in the pilot's headphones. Clockwise is louder, counter-clockwise is quieter.
controls.context: The pilot sets it once at the start so that radio calls can be heard over the engine.

controls.name: FuG 16ZY communications / homing switch (FT / ABST)

positions.name: Ft
positions.text: Radio telephony: normal talking and listening.

positions.name: Abst
positions.text: Tuning for homing: the radio is used together with a ground station to find the direction.

controls.text: This switch sets what the radio does. In position Ft the radio is a normal telephone for talking. In position Abst it tunes to a ground station for direction finding (homing).
controls.context: For normal talking the manual says to use it on Ft together with the frequency positions II, III or IV.

panels.name: Landing gear and flaps indicators
panels.text: Three lamps show where the landing gear and the flaps are. The left and right lamps are for the two main wheels, the middle lamp is for the flaps.
panels.context: The pilot checks them after every gear or flap command. Mechanical indicators in the wings back them up.

controls.name: Landing gear lights (left and right)
controls.text: These two lamps show the state of the main wheels. Red means the gear is up. Green means it is down.
controls.context: Both red means the gear is raised and locked. Both green means it is down and locked, ready for landing.

controls.name: Flaps light (middle)
controls.text: This middle lamp shows the flaps. Red means flaps up. Yellow means the middle take-off position. Green means flaps fully down.
controls.context: The manual notes that the electric lamp only shows full landing or up positions. The wing gauge shows the real angle.

panels.name: Mechanical gear and flap indicators (in the wings)
panels.text: Small mechanical indicators in the wings show the real state of the gear and flaps. The pilot can see them through holes in the wing.
panels.context: They back up the lamps in the cockpit.

controls.name: Flaps position gauge
controls.text: A small gauge seen through a hole in the wing shows the real angle of the flap in degrees.
controls.context: It is the only way to see the take-off flap position exactly.

controls.name: Landing gear position rod
controls.text: A red pin sticks up out of the wing when the gear leg below it is down, and sinks when the gear is up.
controls.context: The pilot looks at the pin to check the right gear is locked.

areas.name: Right console
areas.text: The right side holds the canopy controls, the starter, the flight clock, the gunsight adjustment unit and the electrical circuit breakers.

panels.name: Canopy controls
panels.text: These two controls open and close the canopy, and throw it away in an emergency.
panels.context: The pilot closes the canopy before the engine start.

controls.name: Canopy crank
controls.text: This hand crank opens and closes the canopy (the glass roof over the pilot). Turned clockwise it opens the canopy. Turned counter-clockwise it closes it.
controls.context: The pilot uses it on the ground and before flight. In the game, pulling out the crank handle to move the canopy by hand is not simulated.

controls.name: Canopy jettison lever
controls.text: This lever throws the canopy off the plane with a small explosive charge. It is for emergencies, when the pilot must leave the plane.
controls.context: It is part of the bail-out procedure in the manual's emergency section.

panels.name: Starter switch
panels.text: This switch starts the engine. It sits under a small cover.
panels.context: It is used once the circuit breakers and the throttle are set.

controls.name: Starter switch cover
controls.text: This cover sits over the starter switch so that it cannot be hit by accident. The pilot lifts it before using the switch.
controls.context: It protects the starter switch while the plane flies.

controls.name: Starter switch (Anlasser)
controls.text: This switch starts the engine in two steps. Holding it down spins up a heavy flywheel (a spinning wheel that stores energy). Then the pilot pulls it up and the flywheel is joined to the engine, which turns it to start. The game splits it into a starter power command and a clutch command.
controls.context: The D-9 manual says to press it about 15 to 20 seconds for the flywheel to spin up, then pull it up for the start. It follows the circuit breakers and the throttle at Anlassen.

panels.name: Flight clock
panels.text: The flight clock shows the time and has a stopwatch. A compass correction card is mounted below it.
panels.context: The pilot can time parts of the flight with it.

controls.name: Flight clock start-stop button
controls.text: This button stops and restarts the whole clockwork of the flight clock. It is pushed in while the pilot sets the time and pulled back afterwards.
controls.context: It is used only to set the clock to the right time.

controls.name: Flight clock stopwatch button
controls.text: This button runs the stopwatch of the clock. The first press starts it, the second press stops it, the third press sets it back to zero. A small dial counts up to 15 minutes.
controls.context: The pilot can time a leg of the flight or a turn with it.

controls.name: Flight clock wind/set knob and bezel
controls.text: The clock has a round wind/set knob under its face and a turnable bezel (outer ring). The wind/set knob sets the time while the start-stop button is pushed in. The game names two knobs 'clock_scale' and 'clock_pinion', and the manual does not say which is which.
controls.context: The pilot sets the time before the flight so that the clock matches the mission time.

controls.name: Compass deviation card
controls.text: This card is a small table. It tells the pilot how much the magnetic compass is wrong on different headings.
controls.context: It is a paper aid in the cockpit.

panels.name: EZ 42 adjustment unit (Justierkasten)
panels.text: This box on the right side sets up the gunsight for the height at which the plane flies.
panels.context: A table on its front gives the right setting for each altitude band.

controls.name: Altitude aiming correction knob I
controls.text: Rotary I of the box corrects the sight for the flight altitude. The game names it 'Altitude Aiming Correction Adjusting Knob I'. Rotary II is covered and fixed at 63.
controls.context: The pilot sets the value from the table for his altitude. For example at 9 kilometres rotary I is set to 68.

panels.name: Forward circuit breaker panel
panels.text: This panel holds the main circuit breakers of the plane, behind a flap lid. They switch the main electrical equipment on and off and protect it.
panels.context: The manual's start-up says to turn on all eight of them after pressing the gear Aus button.

controls.name: Circuit breaker cover
controls.text: This flap lid covers the forward circuit breaker panel. The pilot opens it to reach the breakers.
controls.context: It keeps the breakers from being pressed by accident.

controls.name: Circuit breaker panels
controls.text: The right console has two panels of circuit breakers: the forward panel with eight and the additional panel with five.
controls.context: The breakers are explained one by one in these two panels.

controls.name: V350 flaps, trimmer, artificial horizon breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the flaps motor, the tail trim motor and the artificial horizon.
controls.context: Without it the flaps and the trim do not move and the horizon does not work.

controls.name: E16 landing gear breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the landing gear motors.
controls.context: Without it the gear buttons do nothing.

controls.name: D1 pitot heating breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the pitot heating, which warms the small tube outside that measures airspeed so that it does not freeze.
controls.context: The manual says to switch it on in damp air or below freezing.

controls.name: F211 FuG 25a breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the FuG 25a identification unit.
controls.context: The D-9 manual lists that unit as not implemented.

controls.name: F136 FuG 16ZY breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the FuG 16ZY radio.
controls.context: Without it the radio has no power and cannot be used.

controls.name: V24 instruments, lighting, gunsight, compass, starter breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the instruments, the instrument lighting, the gunsight, the compass and the starter.
controls.context: The starter needs it, so it has to be on before the engine start.

controls.name: A4 generator breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the generator, which makes electricity while the engine runs.
controls.context: The generator takes over from the battery once the engine runs.

controls.name: A6 battery breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the battery, which stores electricity for when the engine is off.
controls.context: It supplies power for the engine start.

panels.name: Additional circuit breaker panel
panels.text: This smaller panel holds the breakers for the navigation lights and the fuel and MW-50 pumps.
panels.context: The manual says to switch on the fuel pumps with it before the engine start.

controls.name: C1 navigation lights breaker
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the navigation lights, the coloured lamps on the wing tips.
controls.context: They are lit when the plane flies at night.

controls.name: E14 forward tank fuel pump breaker (Vorn)
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the electric pump in the forward fuel tank.
controls.context: The manual lists it with the other pumps in the start-up.

controls.name: E13 rear tank fuel pump breaker (Hinten)
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the electric pump in the rear fuel tank.
controls.context: The manual lists it with the other pumps in the start-up.

controls.name: E85 external tank fuel pump breaker (Sonder)
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the pump of the drop tank, an extra tank under the fuselage. The game names it 'Auxiliary Tank Pump'.
controls.context: It is only needed when a drop tank is fitted. The manual says to switch it off when the tank is empty.

controls.name: E96 MW-50 valve breaker (MW Anlage)
controls.text: A circuit breaker is a switch that also works as an automatic fuse: if too much current flows, it pops out by itself. It has two buttons, a larger black one with a white dot that switches on and a small red one that switches off. This one is for the MW-50 system, which has to be on before the MW-50 switch works.
controls.context: The manual lists it for use only if necessary.

areas.name: Floor
areas.text: The rudder pedals are on the floor in front of the pilot.

panels.name: Rudder pedals
panels.text: The two pedals steer the plane left and right in the air and on the ground, and their top parts work the wheel brakes.
panels.context: The manual says to check the rudder for full and free movement right after climbing in.

controls.name: Rudder pedals
controls.text: Pushing the left pedal turns the nose left, pushing the right pedal turns it right. The wheel brakes are worked through the same pedals, one wheel at a time.
controls.context: On the ground the pedals steer the plane and brake it. In the air they keep the nose straight in turns.

areas.name: Behind the pilot
areas.text: The oxygen emergency knob is at the pilot's right elbow.

panels.name: Oxygen emergency knob
panels.text: A knob that gives the pilot extra oxygen when breathing becomes hard.
panels.context: It is pressed with the right elbow, as the manual describes.

controls.name: Oxygen emergency knob
controls.text: This knob gives extra oxygen when breathing becomes hard. The pilot presses it several times for short moments with the right elbow. The game offers an ON and an OFF command for it.
controls.context: The manual advises using it at the first sign of breathing trouble in thin air.

areas.name: Stick and throttle
areas.text: The stick is in the right hand and holds the trigger and the bomb release. The throttle is in the left hand, with the flap and gear buttons, the trim switch and the radio button next to it.

panels.name: Control stick (KG 13 grip)
panels.text: The stick steers the plane forward, back, left and right and holds the buttons for the guns and bombs.
panels.context: The manual shows a conventional stick with a trigger and a bomb release button.

controls.name: Control stick
controls.text: Moving the stick back lifts the plane's nose. Moving it forward lowers it. Moving it left or right rolls the plane to that side.
controls.context: On the ground the manual says that pushing the stick forward by about 3 cm unlocks the tailwheel so that the plane can turn.

controls.name: Trigger (all guns)
controls.text: The trigger fires the guns. It works only when the guns master arm switch is on.
controls.context: The D-9 has two MG 131 machine guns above the engine and two MG 151/20 cannons in the wing roots.

controls.name: Button B2 (bomb and rocket release)
controls.text: This button drops the bombs or launches the rockets.
controls.context: The pilot first sets the bomb fusing dial or the main rocket switch. Each press launches one pair of R4M rockets or one BR 21 rocket.

controls.name: Button B1 (outer wing cannons)
controls.text: JoyPro's catalog lists a button B1 for the outer wing cannons. The D-9 manual describes no outer wing guns and no such button.
controls.context: On the Fw 190 A-8 this button fires the outer wing cannons.

controls.name: Trigger guard
controls.text: JoyPro's catalog lists a folding guard over the trigger that keeps the guns safe when closed. The D-9 manual does not describe it.
controls.context: The A-8 manual shows the guard on the A-8's stick.

controls.name: Gun camera button
controls.text: JoyPro's catalog lists a button that runs the gun camera. The D-9 manual only names a gun camera on its electrical diagram and does not describe the button.
controls.context: The camera films while the guns fire, to check hits.

panels.name: Throttle and left-hand controls
panels.text: These controls are under the pilot's left hand: the throttle lever, the switches for the flaps, the landing gear and the stabilizer trim, and the radio button.
panels.context: Everything the pilot needs in a fight can be reached without letting go of the stick.

controls.name: Throttle lever (with Bediengerät, Kommandogerät system)

positions.name: Aus
positions.text: Engine off.

positions.name: Anlassen
positions.text: Engine start and idle.

positions.name: Steigen
positions.text: Climb power.

positions.name: Start
positions.text: Take-off power.

controls.text: Pushing the lever forward gives the engine more power, pulling it back gives less. Other old planes also had levers for the propeller angle, the fuel mixture and the supercharger. Here a mechanical computer, the Bediengerät (called Kommandogerät in earlier Fw 190s), does that. The pilot only picks the boost on the ATA gauge and the computer sets the rest. It works like an automatic gearbox in a car.
controls.context: The lever's marks are Aus (off), Anlassen (start), Steigen (climb) and Start (take-off). The lever carries the range twist grip and the push-to-talk button. The game also names a part 'NGon058' of the throttle, which the manual does not describe.

controls.name: Aus / Anlassen positions
controls.text: At the rear end of the lever's travel are two marks: Aus (off) and Anlassen (start / idle).
controls.context: The lever is set to Anlassen before the starter is used. The manual says to pull it beyond the idle stop to stop the engine.

controls.name: Full power (MW-50)
controls.text: At the front end of the travel the lever gives the strongest power. The manual's power table calls it emergency power or increased take-off power, allowed for only a few minutes.
controls.context: MW-50 injection, which gives extra power, is enabled with its own switch on the left console.

controls.name: Propeller pitch crank
controls.text: JoyPro's catalog lists a crank on the end of the throttle that changes the propeller pitch: Kleiner is finer pitch and higher RPM, Größer coarser pitch and lower RPM. The D-9 manual does not describe it, and the game's D-9 list has no click part for it.
controls.context: In the D-9 the Bediengerät sets the propeller itself.

controls.name: Kommandogerät auto / manual switch

positions.name: Manual
positions.text: Propeller pitch is set by hand.

positions.name: Auto
positions.text: The Kommandogerät sets the propeller pitch.

controls.text: JoyPro's catalog lists a switch for automatic or manual propeller pitch. The D-9 manual does not describe it, and the game's D-9 list has no click part for it.
controls.context: Its place is taken in the D-9 by the MBG emergency handle on the lower front panel.

controls.name: Push-to-talk button
controls.text: This unmarked round button at the base of the throttle turns the radio's transmitter on while it is held. The pilot talks while holding it.
controls.context: It belongs to the FuG 16ZY radio.

controls.name: EZ 42 range twist grip
controls.text: This twist grip on the throttle sets the target range for the gunsight. Cables turn it into the range pointer on the sight. The game calls it 'EZ42 Gunsight Target Distance Control'.
controls.context: The pilot turns it until the ring of the sight just fits around the target. For bombs or rockets the manual says to set it to zero.

controls.name: Horizontal stabilizer trim switch

positions.name: Kopflastig
positions.text: Up: nose-heavy. The motor runs as long as the switch is pressed.

positions.name: Middle
positions.text: The switch springs back here and the trim stays as it is.

positions.name: Schwanzlastig
positions.text: Down: tail-heavy. The motor runs as long as the switch is pressed.

controls.text: This switch tilts the horizontal stabilizer (the small wing at the tail) to trim the plane so it flies straight without constant pressure on the stick. It springs back to the middle.
controls.context: The pilot sets the trim to 0 on the indicator before take-off and corrects it in flight.

controls.name: Horizontal stabilizer trim indicator
controls.text: This small gauge shows how the tail's stabilizer (the fixed part in front of the elevator) is tilted. The mark 0 is the normal position. The scale runs from -5 to +5 degrees, but the plane only uses a part of it.
controls.context: The pilot looks at it after engine start and before take-off to be sure the trim is at 0.

controls.name: Flap buttons (Landeklappen)

positions.name: Ein
positions.text: Flaps up, retracted.

positions.name: Start
positions.text: Take-off position, extended 10 degrees.

positions.name: Aus
positions.text: Landing position, extended 60 degrees.

controls.text: These three push-buttons set the flaps, the parts of the wing that fold down for take-off and landing. The pressed button stays down while the flaps move and pops up when they have arrived.
controls.context: The manual says to set take-off flaps before take-off and to raise the flaps only after the landing gear is up.

controls.name: Landing gear buttons (Rollwerk)

positions.name: Ein
positions.text: Raise the gear. Needs the safety cover to be retracted.

positions.name: Aus
positions.text: Lower the gear.

controls.text: These two push-buttons raise and lower the landing gear. The Ein button raises it. It is under a safety cover that has to be moved aside first. The Aus button lowers it.
controls.context: The manual says the green Rollwerk Aus button must be pressed when entering the cockpit, or the gear retracts when power comes on.

controls.name: Landing gear safety cover
controls.text: This small cover sits over the gear-up button so that the gear cannot be raised by accident, for example on the ground.
controls.context: The manual says to put it back after raising the gear.

controls.name: Landing gear and flaps buttons (group)
controls.text: The five push-buttons on the left console are the flap buttons on the left and the landing gear buttons on the right.
controls.context: The buttons are explained one by one next to this entry.
